title: Technical MCQ Set 02: Collections, SQL Grouping & Deadlocks
description: Covers Java generics erasure, ConcurrentHashMap, SQL HAVING vs WHERE, B-Tree indexes, OS Round Robin, TCP windowing, and Spring DI.

questions.question: What happens when `run()` is called in the following Java snippet?
options: Fails to compile because `finally` cannot throw exceptions
questions.explanation: When a `finally` block throws an uncaught exception while another exception from `try` is propagating out, the `finally` exception replaces/masks the original exception (unlike `try-with-resources`, which attaches suppressed exceptions).

questions.question: What does this Java code print?
questions.explanation: In Java, operands evaluate strictly left-to-right: `i++` evaluates to `5` (then `i` becomes `6`). Next `++i` increments `6` to `7` and evaluates to `7`. Thus `i = 5 + 7 = 12`.

questions.explanation: Fields (instance variables) in Java are resolved at compile time based on the reference type (`Base`, so `b.val == 10`), whereas overridden instance methods use dynamic dispatch based on the runtime object (`Sub`, so `b.getVal() == 20`).

questions.question: How many lines does the following Java 8 Stream snippet print?
questions.explanation: Intermediate Stream operations like `filter()` and `map()` are completely lazy. Because no terminal operation (`collect`, `forEach`, `count`, etc.) is invoked, the pipeline never executes and nothing is printed.

questions.question: Which statement accurately differentiates `ConcurrentHashMap` from `Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())` in Java 8+?
options: `ConcurrentHashMap` allows `null` keys and `null` values, while `HashMap` does not
`ConcurrentHashMap` uses fine-grained CAS + per-bin synchronization instead of locking the entire map on every read/write
`synchronizedMap` outperforms `ConcurrentHashMap` under high multi-threaded read contention
questions.explanation: `ConcurrentHashMap` forbids `null` keys/values (to avoid ambiguity in concurrent `get`), uses weakly consistent non-failing iterators, and locks only individual bucket heads (plus lock-free CAS reads), delivering far higher concurrency.

questions.question: If two threads concurrently execute `count++` 1,000 times each on a `private volatile int count = 0;` field, why can the final value be less than 2,000?
options: `volatile` only prevents instruction reordering on `long` and `double` fields
`volatile` guarantees visibility across threads, NOT atomicity of the compound read-modify-write `count++` operation
`volatile` caches the variable inside thread-local registers permanently
`volatile` throws an unchecked exception on write races
questions.explanation: `count++` comprises three steps: read `count`, add 1, write `count`. `volatile` guarantees memory visibility and happens-before ordering, but does not provide mutual exclusion—use `AtomicInteger` or `synchronized`.

questions.question: When an object implementing `Serializable` is serialized to bytes and deserialized back into memory, what value does a `transient int pin;` field (set to `4821` before serialization) hold after deserialization?
questions.explanation: `transient` excludes a field from Java's default serialization stream; on deserialization, constructors are not run and `transient` primitives receive their type defaults (`0` for `int`, `null` for references).

questions.question: Table `Metrics` has 5 rows where column `latency_ms` holds values `{12, NULL, 18, NULL, 25}`. What does `SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(latency_ms), COUNT(DISTINCT latency_ms) FROM Metrics;` return?
questions.explanation: `COUNT(*)` counts all 5 rows including NULLs; `COUNT(col)` ignores NULLs (returning 3); `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` also ignores NULLs and counts distinct non-null values (3).

questions.question: What is the logical SQL query execution order across clauses?
options: `SELECT -> FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> ORDER BY`
`FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY`
`FROM -> GROUP BY -> WHERE -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY`
`FROM -> HAVING -> GROUP BY -> WHERE -> SELECT -> ORDER BY`
questions.explanation: SQL evaluates `FROM/JOIN` first, filters individual rows in `WHERE`, aggregates groups in `GROUP BY`, filters groups in `HAVING`, projects expressions in `SELECT`, and finally sorts in `ORDER BY`.

questions.question: Why can a relational table physically have at most ONE clustered index, whereas it can have many non-clustered indexes?
options: SQL syntax reserves only one `INDEX` keyword per table
A clustered index dictates the physical storage order of the actual table data rows themselves
Non-clustered indexes cannot be built using B-Trees
Clustered indexes automatically disable foreign key constraints
questions.explanation: Because table data rows can be physically sorted on disk in only one order, a table supports at most one clustered index; non-clustered indexes store separate pointer entries referencing rows.

questions.question: Which mechanism enables a database management system to guarantee both Atomicity (rollback/undo) and Durability (crash recovery/redo) efficiently?
questions.explanation: Write-Ahead Logging writes undo/redo log records to stable storage before flushing modified data pages, allowing uncommitted changes to be rolled back and committed transactions to be replayed after a crash.

questions.question: Three processes all arrive at `t = 0` with burst times: P1 = 5 ms, P2 = 3 ms, P3 = 4 ms. Using Round Robin with time quantum `q = 2 ms` (zero context-switch overhead), what is the completion time of P1?
questions.explanation: Ready queue trace (q=2): [0-2] P1 runs (rem 3, requeued behind P3); [2-4] P2 (rem 1); [4-6] P3 (rem 2); [6-8] P1 (rem 1); [8-9] P2 finishes; [9-11] P3 finishes; [11-12] P1 executes its final 1 ms and completes at 12 ms.

questions.question: A paging system has a TLB lookup time of 10 ns and main memory access time of 100 ns. If the TLB hit ratio is 90% (and page table lives in main memory, 1-level paging), what is the Effective Access Time (EAT)?
questions.explanation: On TLB hit (0.90): 10 ns (TLB) + 100 ns (data) = 110 ns. On TLB miss (0.10): 10 ns (TLB) + 100 ns (page table) + 100 ns (data) = 210 ns. EAT = 0.90*110 + 0.10*210 = 99 + 21 = 120 ns.

questions.question: What characterizes 'thrashing' in a virtual memory operating system?
options: CPU utilization reaches 100% because all threads stay busy executing pure arithmetic
The OS spends more time paging frames in and out of disk than executing actual process instructions
Two processes wait indefinitely on a shared binary semaphore
Network sockets exhaust ephemeral ports due to TIME_WAIT
questions.explanation: When the sum of active working sets exceeds physical RAM, processes continuously page-fault and steal frames from one another, collapsing CPU utilization as disk swap activity dominates.

questions.question: A 1 Mbps link has a one-way propagation delay of 10 ms and transmits 1,000-byte frames using Stop-and-Wait ARQ (negligible ACK size and processing time). What is the approximate link utilization?
questions.explanation: Transmission time Tt = (1,000 * 8 bits) / 10^6 bps = 8 ms. Round-trip propagation 2*Tp = 20 ms. Utilization = Tt / (Tt + 2*Tp) = 8 / (8 + 20) = 8 / 28 = 28.57% ≈ 28.6%.

questions.question: Which pairing of protocol/device to its primary OSI layer is INCORRECT?
options: ARP -> Data Link / Network boundary (resolving IP to MAC)
questions.explanation: TLS/SSL operates above TCP (Layer 4) to provide encryption/session security (historically mapped to Session/Presentation Layers 5–6), never Layer 3 (Network).

questions.question: When deleting a node `X` that has BOTH left and right non-null children in a Binary Search Tree (BST), what node replaces `X` to preserve the BST invariant?
options: Either `X`'s left child directly or `X`'s right child directly
Either the inorder predecessor (max in left subtree) or inorder successor (min in right subtree)
Always the root of the entire BST
The deepest leaf in the entire tree regardless of key value
questions.explanation: Replacing `X` with its inorder successor (leftmost node in right subtree) or inorder predecessor (rightmost node in left subtree) guarantees all left keys stay smaller and all right keys stay larger.

questions.question: Which algorithm finds the shortest path (minimum edge count) between two vertices in an UNWEIGHTED graph?
questions.explanation: BFS explores vertices in non-decreasing order of edge distance from the source, guaranteeing the shortest unweighted path in O(V + E) time.

questions.question: A Java method's control-flow graph has 12 nodes (`N = 12`), 15 directed edges (`E = 15`), and 1 connected component (`P = 1`). What is its McCabe Cyclomatic Complexity?
questions.explanation: McCabe's formula: V(G) = E - N + 2P = 15 - 12 + 2(1) = 5. This means 5 linearly independent execution paths (minimum unit test cases for branch coverage).

questions.question: Why is Constructor Injection preferred over Field Injection (`@Autowired` on a private field) in Spring Boot services?
options: Field injection fails to compile on Java 17+
Constructor injection supports immutable `final` dependencies, guarantees non-null initialization, and simplifies plain JUnit unit testing without starting a Spring container
Constructor injection automatically turns every service into a prototype bean
Field injection disables Spring Data JPA transaction proxies
questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, allows `final` immutable fields, detects circular dependencies eagerly at startup, and lets unit tests instantiate the class via `new Service(mockRepo)` without reflection.

questions.question: By default in JDBC, what is `connection.getAutoCommit()` set to, and what is required to execute two `UPDATE` statements atomically as one transaction?
options: `true`; call `connection.setAutoCommit(false)` before the statements, then `commit()` or `rollback()`
`false`; JDBC automatically batches all updates until `close()`
questions.explanation: JDBC connections default to `autoCommit = true`, committing each statement individually. For multi-statement atomicity, set `setAutoCommit(false)`, execute updates, and invoke `commit()` (or `rollback()` inside `catch`).

questions.question: Using the Master Theorem, solve the recurrence `T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n` (with `T(1) = 1`).
questions.explanation: Here a = 4, b = 2, f(n) = n. Critical exponent c = log_b(a) = log_2(4) = 2, so n^c = n^2. Since f(n) = O(n^(2 - epsilon)), Case 1 of the Master Theorem yields Theta(n^2).

questions.question: A REST client sends a valid JSON payload with an expired JWT bearer token, and the API gateway rejects it due to missing/expired authentication. Which HTTP status code is semantically accurate?
questions.explanation: `401 Unauthorized` denotes unauthenticated or expired/invalid credentials; `403 Forbidden` denotes an authenticated user lacking permission for the resource.

questions.question: In SQL, what is the key difference between `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` when two employees tie for the 2nd highest salary?
options: `RANK()` assigns both rank 2 and the next employee rank 3; `DENSE_RANK()` assigns rank 4
`RANK()` assigns both rank 2 and skips rank 3 (next is 4); `DENSE_RANK()` assigns both rank 2 and next is 3
`DENSE_RANK()` requires an explicit `GROUP BY` clause, whereas `RANK()` does not
`RANK()` ignores NULL values automatically, whereas `DENSE_RANK()` fails on NULLs
questions.explanation: On ties `{100, 90, 90, 80}` descending: `RANK()` gives `1, 2, 2, 4` (leaves gaps); `DENSE_RANK()` gives `1, 2, 2, 3` (no gaps); `ROW_NUMBER()` gives `1, 2, 3, 4`.
